v04.text: Russia. A tiny village deep in eastern Siberia dropped below minus 67 degrees back in 1933.

v05.text: Around 500 people still live there today, and a perfectly normal January averages minus 46.

v06.text: Your kitchen freezer sits at minus 18. Only Antarctica goes colder, minus 89 at Vostok station.

v07.text: And the school stays open until minus 52. The older pupils keep going until minus 56.

v08.text: Pack a second coat. Follow us.

geo.highlight_note: Russia (answer) — fill pulse on the reveal; the village is a pin, not a shape

research.topic: Coldest permanently inhabited place: Oymyakon, Sakha Republic, Russia — −67.7 °C on 6 February 1933 (WMO-recognised northern-hemisphere record); ~500 residents; January mean about −46 °C; school closes below −52 °C (grades 1–5), older pupils below −56 °C; Vostok −89.2 °C is the planet's record (uninhabited station).

myths.myth: Canada or Greenland must be coldest because they are nearer the pole.
myths.reality: Oymyakon sits in a Siberian valley basin that traps draining cold air; the continental interior gets colder than coastal Arctic Canada or Greenland's inhabited coast.

landscape.our_gap: Cold-town Shorts show the frozen-eyelashes clip and stop; none puts the village on a night map next to a freezer and an Antarctic station on one scale.
